'''Simon Phillips Norton''' (28 February 1952 – 13 February 2019)<ref name="Obit">{{Cite web |date=15 February 2019 |title=Simon Norton, mathematical prodigy who became the subject of the biography 'The Genius in my Basement' – obituary |url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/obituaries/2019/02/15/simon-norton-mathematical-prodigy-became-subject-biography-genius/ |website=[[The Daily Telegraph|The Telegraph]]}}</ref> was a mathematician in [[Cambridge]], England, who worked on finite [[simple group]]s.

==Education==
Simon Norton was born into a [[Sephardi]] family of [[History of the Jews in Iraq|Iraqi descent]], the youngest of three brothers.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.thejc.com/news/obituaries/obituary-simon-norton-jllydqle|title=Obituary: Simon Norton|first=Gloria|last=Tessler|date=28 March 2019|newspaper=[[The Jewish Chronicle]]}}</ref>

From 1964 he was a [[King's Scholar]] at [[Eton College]], where he earned a reputation as an eccentric mathematical genius and was taught by [[Norman Routledge]]. He obtained an external first-class degree in Pure Mathematics at the University of London while still at the school, commuting to [[Royal Holloway, University of London|Royal Holloway College]].

He also represented the United Kingdom at the [[International Mathematical Olympiad]] thrice consecutively starting from 1967, winning a gold medal each time and two special prizes in 1967 and 1969.<ref>{{Cite web |title=International Mathematical Olympiad - Simon Phillips Norton |url=https://www.imo-official.org/participant_r.aspx?id=10021 |website=[[International Mathematical Olympiad]]}}</ref>

He then went up to [[Trinity College, Cambridge]], and achieved a first in the final examinations.

==Career and life==
He stayed at Cambridge, working on [[finite group]]s. Norton was one of the authors of the [[ATLAS of Finite Groups]]. He constructed the [[Harada–Norton group]] and in 1979,  together with [[John Horton Conway|John Conway]] proved there is a connection between the [[Monster group]] and the [[j-invariant|''j''-function]] in number theory. They dubbed this "[[monstrous moonshine]]", and made some conjectures later proved by [[Richard Borcherds]]. Norton also made several early discoveries in [[Conway's Game of Life]],<ref>{{citation |last=Poundstone |first=William |title=The Recursive Universe: Cosmic Complexity and the Limits of Scientific Knowledge |page=7 |year=1985 |publisher=Contemporary Books |isbn=978-0-8092-5202-2 |author-link=William Poundstone}}</ref> and invented the game [[Snort (game)|Snort]].

In 1985, Cambridge University did not renew his contract.

Norton is the subject of the biography ''The Genius in My Basement'', written by his Cambridge tenant, [[Alexander Masters]],<ref>{{Citation | last = Masters | first = Alexander | author-link = Alexander Masters | publication-date = 1 September 2011 | title = The Genius in My Basement | year = 2012 | publisher = [[HarperCollins]] | publication-place = London | isbn = 978-0-00-724338-9 | lccn = 2011535364 | oclc = 739420610 | url-access = registration | url = https://archive.org/details/simongeniusinmyb0000mast }}</ref> which describes his eccentric lifestyle and his life-long obsession with buses. He was also an occasional contributor to ''[[Word Ways: The Journal of Recreational Linguistics]]''.

Norton was very interested in transport issues and was a member of Subterranea Britannica. He coordinated the local group of the [[Campaign for Better Transport (United Kingdom)]], and had done so since the organisation was known as Transport 2000, writing most of the newsletter for the local Cambridge group<ref>{{cite web| url= https://cambsbettertransport.neocities.org/ |title= Cambridgeshire Campaign for Better Transport Homepage | date= 2019 | website= Archive of the Cambridgeshire Campaign for Better Transport  | publisher= Cambridgeshire Campaign for Better Transport | access-date= 2022-04-06}}</ref> and tirelessly campaigning for efficient, inclusive and environmentally friendly public transport in the region and across the United Kingdom.

He collapsed and died in north London, aged 66, of a heart condition on 13 February 2019.<ref name=Obit/><ref>{{Cite news |last=Masters |first=Alexander |date=22 February 2019 |title=Simon Norton obituary |url=https://www.theguardian.com/education/2019/feb/22/simon-norton-obituary |access-date=22 July 2024 |work=[[The Guardian]] |language=en-GB |issn=0261-3077}}</ref>
